A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and retain matching core methods and experiments. The complete documents, including their figures, tables, equations and appendices, support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Bleeding Edge scaling experiments, an 894M-parameter extrapolation experiment, and language-modeling analyses in Section 5 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds RT-1 world-modeling experiments and measurements relating world-model loss to generated-video quality.

M1.justification: The existing WM-Token, BC-Token and BC-CNN procedures and scaling-fit methods are retained. The added RT-1 experiments introduce VQVAE image tokenizers, whereas the original embodied experiments use VQGANs. This is a limited tokenizer-component adaptation, without redesigning the transformer learning procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds real-world robotic manipulation through the RT-1 dataset, extending the embodied experiments beyond Bleeding Edge. It also analyzes previously published BC results for NetHack, Bank Heist, Breakout and Space Invaders, explicitly as a meta-analysis rather than new environment runs. The Bleeding Edge, Shakespeare and BookCorpus coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The existing architecture comparisons and fitting-method comparisons are retained. No competing method is newly evaluated against the authors' models in a matched comparison. The Tuyls et al. meta-analysis supplies evidence about loss and return, rather than adding a baseline to the authors' experiments.

E3.justification: New protocols include the RT-1 sweep over five tokenization resolutions and 0.08M–0.99M-parameter models, with two-step sequences and four action dimensions discretized into 500 buckets. Appendix D adds evaluation using 1,024 ten-second generated videos and FVD/LPIPS across checkpoints. The retained Bleeding Edge splits and tabulated training settings are unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 5.3 adds a direct robotics sensitivity study of whether tokens per image affect scaling coefficients, supplementing the retained language analogies. Section 2.2 and Appendix D add analyses testing whether pre-training loss tracks online return and world-model video quality. These substantially expand the evidence addressing mechanism and proxy validity.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly reports three repeated runs per VQVAE for the new RT-1 analysis and displays individual coefficient estimates in Figure 12. v1 has no corresponding replication analysis. This is a localized addition; confidence intervals and significance tests are not added, and increased repetition of the retained experiments is not established.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the original scaling and extrapolation findings are retained. New results include RT-1 example model-size exponents of 0.56 at 16 tokens and 0.65 at 256 tokens (Figure C.2), loss-return correlations from -0.98 to -0.94 (Figure 2), and correlations of 0.83 with FVD and 0.77 with LPIPS (Figure 3). Figure 1 newly labels the BC-Token data exponent as 0.78, conflicting with the retained 0.68 in Table 1.

T1.justification: Equation 6 corrects the model- and data-size scaling exponents from -a and -b to a and b. A new footnote derives a + b = 1 from C = 6ND, although its final proportionality is incorrectly written as N proportional to D^(1-a). The remaining mathematical framework is retained.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same central claims: compute-optimal scaling laws occur in world modeling and BC, tokenizer compression affects their coefficients, and architecture changes the optimal model/data allocation. The added experiments support these existing headline contributions.

C2.justification: Section 2.2 adds substantive arguments for treating loss as a performance proxy, attributes earlier weak-correlation findings to finite-data and overfitting settings, and discusses how improved prediction could reflect richer behavioral and environmental understanding. Appendix A.1 newly explains that 256-token reconstructions miss details such as enemy health bars. The general limitations in Section 6 remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 supplements the existing hyperparameter tables with previously undisclosed learning-rate sweep procedures and tokenizer-resolution selection rationale. Appendices C–D document RT-1 preprocessing, the VQVAE implementation source, 40,000 tokenizer updates with batches of 128, transformer settings, and video-evaluation procedures. These are substantial documentation additions, without establishing that the original experiments were rerun.

R1.justification: v2 adds Hussenot et al. (2021) and Li et al. (2024) when discussing weak relationships between validation loss and policy performance. It also explicitly claims first-time study of world-model scaling and develops its relationship to Tuyls et al. through the meta-analysis. Most cited works and the broader positioning are retained.

P1.justification: Related Work becomes Background, with separate related-work and performance-proxy subsections. The extended related-work appendix is incorporated into the main text, and the remaining appendices are reorganized and relabeled. There are local rewrites and expanded explanations, but most existing methodological, results and concluding prose is preserved.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 2, 3, 12, C.1 and C.2 and Table C.1, moves the gameplay montage from appendix Figure 9 to main-text Figure 5, and adds coefficient annotations to retained plots. A new Microsoft report format changes typography, spacing, headers, footers and figure placement throughout. Some new annotations contain errors, including the exponent 85 in Figure 11.

improvement.justification: v1 supported the tokenizer effect through two different Bleeding Edge setups and language analogies, while largely motivating pre-training loss as a convenient intermediate signal. v2 substantially strengthens both foundations through a repeated, five-resolution robotics study and empirical loss-versus-quality analyses, including direct measurements on its world models. These additions improve the support and generality of the central conclusions. New exponent-label errors, notably Figures 1 and 11, reduce reporting precision but do not outweigh these substantial evidential gains.
